name: option-maybe
intent: Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time.
problem: A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.
context: Lookups, parsing, searches, optional configuration, nullable database columns and any API whose result may legitimately not exist - wherever the language can express absence as a type (Option/Maybe/Optional, a nullable type, a union with undefined) or a convention can carry it. It pays off at module and service boundaries, in chains of partial steps, and wherever 'absent' must stay distinguishable from a legitimate empty, zero or falsey value.
benefits: Absence is in the type: the value cannot be used without handling the empty case, so a forgotten null check becomes a compile error, a warning or at least a visible branch instead of a runtime failure.

No in-band signalling: 'absent' no longer has to be encoded as a sentinel (-1, empty string, out-of-band enum) that can collide with a legitimate value - and unlike a null reference, a real option type nests, so 'no result' and 'the result is nothing' stay distinguishable.
Partial computations compose: map/flatMap/and_then/?/?. chain lookups and transformations and short-circuit at the first absence, instead of nesting if-null pyramids at every step.
Signatures become honest about partiality, and the default policy (orElse/getOrElse/value_or/??/?:) is stated once, at the point where the product decision is made rather than buried in the producer.
Both branches are cheap to test: the empty case is an ordinary value that can be constructed, injected, asserted on and serialized, with no mock returning null and no exception to provoke.

Conversion is local: the boundary from the nullable world (a map lookup, a database column, an interop call returning null) into the option happens once, in one adapter, and the core stays free of null.
tradeoffs: Wrapper contagion: Option spreads through the types of everything it touches, so a function that returned T now returns Option<T> and every caller up the chain has to adapt.

Verbosity without sugar: in languages without ?/for-comprehension/?. the happy path turns into a chain of combinators, and without a native type a hand-written wrapper plus constructors has to be maintained.

Representation cost: heap-allocated wrappers (java.util.Optional on hot paths, boxed Maybe values, classic Maybe classes in C++) cost compared with a nullable pointer or a bool out-parameter, while Rust, Swift and std::optional flatten the common cases to zero overhead.

Two absence mechanisms coexist during and after migration (null plus the wrapper type): every boundary between them is a place where an absence can be turned back into a null, so the discipline is ongoing.
Escape hatches (unwrap, get, value!, !!, !) reintroduce the crash one frame later; without a convention that keeps them to tests and proven invariants, Option becomes signature decoration.
It cannot say why: Option records only that nothing is there, so callers that must branch on a reason need Either/Result - over-using Option for error paths loses the diagnosis.
Nesting is not universally available: nullable-type languages (Kotlin T?, C# string?) cannot distinguish outer from inner absence, so those cases need a separate wrapper or a different model.

participants.responsibility: Holds either a present value or the absence marker; both states are well formed by construction and the payload that is not active is unreachable through the constructors.
Returns the wrapper instead of null or a sentinel, stating in its signature that it may not produce a value, and does not invent a default.
Consumes the wrapper by taking a handler for the present case and a handler or default for the absent case, so handling is complete and happens in one place.
Names the policy for the absent case at the call site: default value, alternative computation, propagation, or a reason-bearing failure.

participants.role: Boundary adapter (Option(x), fromNullable, toOption, comma-ok check)
participants.responsibility: Converts between the nullable world (null returns, missing keys, database columns, interop) and the wrapper in one place, so null never travels deeper into the code.

use_cases: Lookups that can miss: configuration keys, cache entries, registry entries, map/dictionary access - either through the language's two-value form or an Optional-returning accessor.
Parsing and conversion (integers, dates, URLs, decimal numbers, external identifiers) where 'no valid value' is a legitimate answer rather than an error.
Searches over collections and structures (find, first, min/max, binary search, regex match, tree traversal) where a miss is part of the contract.
Genuinely optional data: middle names, second addresses, unset feature flags, optional protocol fields - as opposed to missing state, which is a domain error.
Chains of partial steps (look up user, then their company, then its billing address) where any hop may be absent and the whole chain should collapse to 'nothing'.
Boundaries from nullable interfaces: a database column admits NULL, a legacy or interop API returns null or -1, a deserialized document lacks a field - converted once at the adapter.
Container and stream operations that can be empty (head, pop, next, dequeue, min) and should report emptiness instead of throwing or returning a sentinel.

Rust's standard library uses std::option::Option<T> with Some(T) and None for optional values; its map and pattern-matching APIs let lookup or parsing pipelines stop at absence without a null pointer.

Java SE's java.util.Optional<T> is a production API for method results that may be absent: ofNullable converts a nullable boundary value, map/flatMap compose follow-up work, and orElse/orElseThrow make the exit policy explicit.

Scala's standard-library scala.Option[A] models Some/None and documents map, flatMap, and for-comprehensions for chained partial steps; its API also demonstrates wrapping a Java HashMap lookup so a missing key becomes None.
avoid_when: The absence is an error the caller must diagnose: use Result/Either (or a well-designed exception) so the reason travels - Option deliberately discards it.
Every input has a total answer: a partial signature misrepresents the function exactly as much as a null does, and adds noise.
A Null Object, Special Case object or empty collection already models the absence and answers with neutral behaviour, so no call site needs a branch.

The language has no type-level support and the convention is already unambiguous and checked: a required non-null pointer or an out-parameter with a bool return is simpler than a hand-written Maybe struct.
The value is consumed in a hot loop where the wrapper allocation dominates (per-element Optional in a parsing inner loop); use a primitive sentinel locally and wrap at the boundary.
Present and absent are the same to the caller (counting, existence-only checks): a bool or an empty collection is the honest type.
anti_patterns: Optional everywhere - parameters, fields, collections - so absence gets a second encoding beside null and every call site pays a wrapper tax (Java's own API note limits Optional to method return positions).
Option as decoration: unwrap/get/!!/! called immediately after the call, so the absence still crashes, only one frame later and with a longer signature.
Returning Option to avoid choosing a default, while every caller immediately applies the same getOrElse constant: a total signature with a documented default would be honest.
Mixed channels for one operation (null on one path, empty Option on another, an exception on a third), so no caller can know what to check.
Using Option where Either/Result is required: erasing the failure reason turns a diagnosable validation failure into a silent 'not found'.
Collapsing absence into falsiness (undefined, null, 0, '', false tested with one truthiness check), which conflates legitimate falsey values with the missing case.
design_principles: Make partiality explicit in the type: a total function over Some | None instead of a partial function over T with an unwritten precondition.
No in-band signalling: never overload a domain value as a marker for absence.
Make the empty case impossible to forget: the only routes to the inner value are destructive (match/fold/getOrElse), so the decision is forced by the compiler or by the shape of the API.
Composition over nested control flow: chain partial steps with map/flatMap and short-circuit at the first absence.
Trust boundaries: convert nullable external data once, at the edge where the nullability is known, and keep the core null-free.
The caller owns the fallback: the producer reports absence, the consumer decides the default, the alternative computation or the propagation.
best_practices: Return Option from functions that can legitimately produce nothing; return Either/Result (or throw) where the caller needs a reason.
Treat Option as a return-type contract: prefer a required value, an explicit default or an overload for parameters and fields.
Never construct the empty case out of a value that means something else (0, -1, '', NaN); use the real empty constructor and keep sentinels out of the type.

Use the language-native form (Option[T], T?, T | undefined, std::optional, Optional<T>) and let exhaustiveness checking or flow analysis enforce the handling instead of hand-rolling a Maybe class beside it.
Keep unwrap-style accessors (unwrap, get, value!, !!, !) for tests and for invariants you can prove at that line; provide getOrElse/orElse as the production exits.
Convert null into the wrapper at the boundary (Option(x), fromNullable, toOption, ?. ) and convert back only at the outermost edge, in one adapter.
Keep chains shallow enough to read: split long pipelines or name intermediate steps; a combinator chain longer than a screen hides the control flow it replaced.
When the caller must distinguish absent from invalid, switch to Either/Result instead of layering a reason onto Option.
sources: Option/maybe type as catalogued in the functional-programming tradition (functional-catalog): a polymorphic type with one empty constructor and one wrapping constructor, data Maybe a = Nothing | Just a in Haskell, found in the ML family and used as the standard example of a sum type and a monad - see Wikipedia, Option type (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_type) and HaskellWiki, Maybe (https://wiki.haskell.org/Maybe) for the canonical definition, the type equation A + 1 and the comparison to NULL/union in imperative languages.
